1.pericope_label: O give thanks unto the Lord; call upon his name: make known his deeds among the people... He is the Lord our God: his judgments are in all the earth

schools.summary: Delitzsch classes this as the first of the Hodu-psalms and traces its relation to the festival song in the chronicler, recording that Hitzig reverses the dependence; Ellicott rejects the traditional reading of the strength as the ark, taking the verb as enquire after and the strength as the manifestation of power in the deeds about to be recited.

Gill turns each imperative inward, confession covering God's greatness and the worshipper's own sins alike, and reads Jehovah as self-existence itself, incommunicable to any creature; Calvin narrows the subject deliberately, since the wonders meant are not the sun and the seasons but the free adoption of one people, so that the psalm addresses believers only.

Clarke accepts David's hand in the substance while judging the whole enlarged at the return from Babylon, and keeps the seeking devotional and personal; Wesley agrees that the strength means the ark and glosses the face as the gracious presence.

Henry enumerates seven duties in the opening verses with a reason for each, holding that praying for further mercy is itself an acknowledgment of mercy received; Spurgeon presses the missionary edge and warns against singing for the music's sake.
Augustine begins from the borrowed Hallelujah and takes the confession commanded here to mean praise rather than acknowledgment of sin.

debates.question: What is the strength that is to be sought?

positions.view: The ark, called the strength of God because his power was shown by it at Jordan and Jericho.
Not the ark at all; the verb means enquire after, and the strength is the divine power displayed in the deeds now to be recited.
Grace, the strength of the Spirit to work in us what is good.
A personal seeking of reconciliation, to be a man's chief business.

debates.question: Who wrote the psalm, and in what form?

positions.view: David in substance, the whole probably enlarged at the restoration from Babylon.
The psalm is prior and the chronicler's festival song draws on it, though the reverse has been argued.

outliers.note: Insists the psalm does not celebrate the government of the world, as the preceding one did, but only the adoption of Israel, and so is addressed to none but true believers.
Notes that the opening verse stands word for word in the prophets and was apparently one of the recognized doxologies of the Hebrew Church.

themes: O give thanks unto the Lord; call upon his name: make known his deeds among the people.
Sing unto him, sing psalms unto him: talk ye of all his wondrous works.
Glory ye in his holy name: let the heart of them rejoice that seek the Lord.
Seek the Lord, and his strength: seek his face evermore.
Remember his marvellous works that he hath done; his wonders, and the judgments of his mouth;
O ye seed of Abraham his servant, ye children of Jacob his chosen.
He is the Lord our God: his judgments are in all the earth.

8.pericope_label: He hath remembered his covenant for ever, the word which he commanded to a thousand generations... Saying, Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm

schools.summary: Delitzsch renders the phrase as men of number, men easily counted, and reads the following verb as setting their dependence on successive hosts in a relation of cause and effect; Ellicott treats the Hebrew words for law and covenant as synonyms here and points the protection to the incidents concerning Sarah and Rebekah.

Gill reads the word law as bearing on God rather than on men, so that the covenant has the force of law with respect to God himself, who has laid himself under obligation by grace, and takes the anointed for all believers.

Clarke adds only that all appearances were against the patriarchs, and widens the anointed to the whole nation as a kingdom of priests; Wesley names the three patriarchs and explains the title from their consecration and prophetic converse with God.

Henry counts the ratifications as oath, law and everlasting covenant, works the patriarchs' exposure into three heads, and draws from the rebuking of kings that God's anointed prophets are dearer to him than anointed kings; Spurgeon grounds the exhortation to remember in the fact that God has remembered first.

debates.question: Who are the anointed ones that must not be touched?

positions.view: The three patriarchs, consecrated and called prophets from God's converse with them.
Possibly the whole people, a kingdom of priests and kings.
The term is not technical here, since they were never actually anointed, but is justified by its use of the covenant people as a whole.
All believers, anointed with the oil of grace.

debates.question: In what sense is the promise called a law?

positions.view: It binds God, not man; by grace he has laid himself under obligation.
It is a covenant rather than a bare promise because something was required on man's part.
It carries the authority of a law, a proclamation that will stand though heaven and earth pass away.
The two Hebrew words appear here to be simple synonyms.

outliers.note: Sets out the land of Canaan as a type at length, prepared and furnished and entered only through many battles, answering to the promised inheritance.
Reads the successive migrations grammatically, as cause and effect between the patriarchs' smallness and their dependence on one people's hospitality after another.

themes: He hath remembered his covenant for ever, the word which he commanded to a thousand generations.
Which covenant he made with Abraham, and his oath unto Isaac;
And confirmed the same unto Jacob for a law, and to Israel for an everlasting covenant:
Saying, Unto thee will I give the land of Canaan, the lot of your inheritance:
When they were but a few men in number; yea, very few, and strangers in it.
When they went from one nation to another, from one kingdom to another people;
He suffered no man to do them wrong: yea, he reproved kings for their sakes;
Saying, Touch not mine anointed, and do my prophets no harm.

16.pericope_label: Moreover he called for a famine upon the land: he brake the whole staff of bread... He turned their heart to hate his people, to deal subtilly with his servants

schools.summary: Ellicott is unusually candid on the clause about the iron, weighing syntax, verb gender, the ancient versions and the parallelism against each other, and sharpens the second verb of the release to purified, God proving Joseph innocent by enabling him to foretell the dreams; Delitzsch explains the oppression as God's work only indirectly, the might he gave his people exciting Egyptian jealousy.

Gill supplies the untold detail of galling fetters, catalogues Joseph's offices and makes each a figure of Christ, and denies that God put any hatred into the Egyptians, saying only that he did not restrain it.

Clarke distinguishes the two clauses about the word and prefers the passive rendering of the hardening, explaining the change politically as curtailment once the Hebrews grew too strong; Wesley reads the word as purging Joseph of the calamities cast upon him, and compresses the hardening to God suffering their heart to be turned.

Henry asks in what character the man went who was to prepare a reception for the church and answers that he went as a slave and then a prisoner, and holds that all judgments are at God's call and no place exempt; Spurgeon presses the broken staff and turns the multiplying into the proverb that oppression multiplies.

debates.question: How is God said to turn the Egyptians' heart?

positions.view: He put no hatred in, but withheld restraint and did the things which occasioned it.
He suffered their heart to be turned.
The verb is better taken passively; the change was a policy adopted once the Hebrews grew strong.
Indirectly his work, in that the might he gave Israel excited the jealousy that became oppression.

debates.question: What does it mean that the word tried him?

positions.view: Better purified: God proved Joseph innocent of the charge by giving him the interpretation.
The interpretation given to the butler and baker, or the report of it reaching Pharaoh.
The first clause is the prison dreams, the second Pharaoh's, called the oracle of the Lord because sent by him.
There is a set time when God's word comes for the comfort of those who trust it.

outliers.note: Answers the difficulty of divine hardening with the analogy of the sun, which softens wax and hardens clay and is blamed for neither.
Lays out the evidence for and against the proverbial rendering that the iron entered into Joseph's soul without concealing that it cuts both ways.

themes: Moreover he called for a famine upon the land: he brake the whole staff of bread.
He sent a man before them, even Joseph, who was sold for a servant:
Whose feet they hurt with fetters: he was laid in iron:
Until the time that his word came: the word of the Lord tried him.
The king sent and loosed him; even the ruler of the people, and let him go free.
He made him lord of his house, and ruler of all his substance:
To bind his princes at his pleasure; and teach his senators wisdom.
Israel also came into Egypt; and Jacob sojourned in the land of Ham.
And he increased his people greatly; and made them stronger than their enemies.
He turned their heart to hate his people, to deal subtilly with his servants.

26.pericope_label: He sent Moses his servant; and Aaron whom he had chosen... That they might observe his statutes, and keep his laws. Praise ye the Lord

schools.summary: Ellicott states the crux of the darkness verse squarely, rejects the usual solutions in turn, and adopts a proposed emendation making the plague a figure of the moral blindness the Egyptians showed throughout; he also notes the added insect name as a poetical synonym and says the reason given in the histories for the cloud has been lost sight of.

Gill numbers each plague in its Exodus order while reading each as a type of the vials poured on spiritual Egypt, defends the spoiling of the Egyptians as equitable payment, and raises the difficulty that the pillar stood upright rather than covering the camp.

Clarke offers a lost letter or the innocence of Moses and Aaron as remedies for the darkness verse, notes that the smiting of the vines is absent from Exodus, and ends with a granite fragment of the rock at Horeb which he makes the one remaining emblem of Christ in creation; Wesley takes the unrebelling pair to be Moses and Aaron and calls the absence of a single stumbler wonderful.
Spurgeon exults over the cloud and the fire, and observes that the psalm deliberately selects the happier theme and dwells only on covenant love, though the tale of Israel's sin is as extraordinary.

debates.question: Who rebelled not against his word?

positions.view: Moses and Aaron, who obeyed the command they received.
A letter has dropped from the verb, and the sense is that they did not observe his word.
None of the usual solutions will serve; an emendation yielding that God darkened them so they might not discern his tokens is preferable.
A canopy against the sun.
The pillar stood upright and went before them, so either it sheltered them only at rest or there were several clouds.
The reason assigned in the histories has been lost sight of and the pillar has simply become a canopy.

outliers.note: Describes a granite fragment of the Horeb rock lying on his desk and builds a geological emblem of Christ from the composition of the stone.
Runs a sustained application of each plague to the vials poured out on spiritual Egypt alongside his ordinary exposition.

themes: He sent Moses his servant; and Aaron whom he had chosen.
They shewed his signs among them, and wonders in the land of Ham.
He sent darkness, and made it dark; and they rebelled not against his word.
He turned their waters into blood, and slew their fish.
Their land brought forth frogs in abundance, in the chambers of their kings.
He spake, and there came divers sorts of flies, and lice in all their coasts.
He gave them hail for rain, and flaming fire in their land.
He smote their vines also and their fig trees; and brake the trees of their coasts.
He spake, and the locusts came, and caterpillers, and that without number,
And did eat up all the herbs in their land, and devoured the fruit of their ground.
He smote also all the firstborn in their land, the chief of all their strength.
He brought them forth also with silver and gold: and there was not one feeble person among their tribes.
Egypt was glad when they departed: for the fear of them fell upon them.
He spread a cloud for a covering; and fire to give light in the night.
The people asked, and he brought quails, and satisfied them with the bread of heaven.
He opened the rock, and the waters gushed out; they ran in the dry places like a river.
For he remembered his holy promise, and Abraham his servant.
And he brought forth his people with joy, and his chosen with gladness:
And gave them the lands of the heathen: and they inherited the labour of the people;
That they might observe his statutes, and keep his laws. Praise ye the Lord.
